paras: The lynching of Joseph Snyder took place on December 27, 1880, when a crowd seized Snyder from a detective at Santee's Mills, near Bethlehem in Northampton County, Pennsylvania, and hanged him from a chestnut tree. Snyder, a boarder accused of killing Jacob and Annie Gogle with an axe hours earlier, was hanged while the coroner's jury sat upstairs in the victims' house. Newspapers called it the first lynching in Pennsylvania, and no one was indicted after a judge told the county grand jury the killing was murder.

Snyder, described as 24 or about 28 years old and an ore-mine worker, boarded with the Gogle family, whom the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer called "a quiet German family". According to the Easton and Lancaster accounts, he had pressed unwanted attentions on the Gogles' daughter Alice, and after a quarrel on Saturday he was told to pay his board and leave. In the night of December 26 the couple were killed in their bed with an axe, and Snyder was accused of attempting to assault Alice before alarming neighbors with a story of burglars.

Snyder disappeared before daylight, and Detective Yohe found him hiding under straw in a neighbor's barn, handcuffed him, and brought him back to the house followed by a crowd shouting "Hang him!" Questioned by the Rev. D. F. Brendle of Bethlehem, Snyder was reported to have answered "Yes, I did" when asked whether he had committed the murders. When Coroner Uhler took his jury upstairs, the crowd pushed the detective aside, put a rope around Snyder's neck, and dragged him out of the house to a chestnut tree on the creek bank.

Yohe pulled Snyder from under the limb three times and was lifted off the ground with him when a crowd of about 100 hauled on the rope, according to the Lancaster account. An Allentown wire report added that Yohe fired at one of the ringleaders without effect. The Lancaster paper reported that Snyder confessed under the tree to having killed the parents in revenge after failing to rape Alice, while the Allentown dispatch gave his motive as removing their opposition to his courtship. The body was cut down and taken to the county poorhouse, where death was found to have been caused by strangulation.

The coroner's jury found that the Gogles died from blows of an axe "in the hands of Joseph Snyder," and no arrests were made on the day of the lynching. A December 28 dispatch said District Attorney Anstett had issued warrants for the active lynchers but feared no jury would convict. An Easton dispatch of January 6 reported instead that nothing had been done before Anstett's term ended, that his own father had taken part, and that public opinion opposed prosecution. The same dispatch said the hanging was done by Bethlehem men rather than neighboring farmers.

In February 1881 Judge Meyers charged the grand jury at Easton that Snyder's death was murder and that the court would act if the jury did not. The grand jury adjourned without taking up the lynching, and one juror said it was not mentioned in its deliberations.

The story ran in white papers across the country within a day, from Pennsylvania and Delaware to Minnesota and West Virginia, with headlines such as "Summary Vengeance on a Pennsylvania Murderer" and "A Villain's Fate." Several papers called it the first lynching known in Pennsylvania, and early accounts dwelt on the murders and praised the detective's efforts. No paper gave a race for Snyder; the Easton dispatch described him as "a German by birth."

Editorial opinion divided over whether the lynching should be punished. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer called the county's defiance of the law "very disgraceful" and urged Anstett to prosecute, noting that Easton papers had defended the lynching by pointing to murderers who had escaped the gallows. The Daily Astorian in Oregon granted that lynching was wrong but blamed "the trickeries of law," and the Juniata Sentinel attributed the lynching to local courts so lenient that trials were "a mockery of justice." Coverage of the grand jury's inaction in early 1881 was brief, and a Middleburg paper remarked that no one had expected the lynchers to be indicted.
